name: Wafer

claims.claim_text: A single chip is rarely made in one country: the silicon wafer may be produced in one place, diced in another, tested in a third and packaged in a fourth, which is why data sheets commonly state that a part is manufactured in one or more of several listed countries.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why you often see in the data sheet manufactured in one or more of the following countries.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Olive-a The World

claims.claim_text: Analog and power semiconductor fabs continue to run mature 180 nm and 250 nm feature sizes on 4-inch wafers because those products gain nothing from finer geometries.
claims.quote_verbatim: They can still make 4-inch wafers making 180, 250 nanometer feature sets.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Girl Power

claims.claim_text: A power chip die of roughly half a millimetre square yields on the order of 200 die on a 4-inch wafer, which remains commercially viable even with manual wafer handling.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the die itself is maybe half a millimeter by half a millimeter across. And you can get 200 chips on a wafer, even at 4 inches, even having people sling them.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Girl Power

claims.claim_text: Around 2010 a single prototype wafer run cost roughly $7,500, and sharing that run with other customers lowered the per-participant cost in the same way that sharing a panel lowers batch PCB prices, provided all participants use the same process.
claims.quote_verbatim: to get a wafer, it's about $7,500 right now. Right. But if you're bundled together with other people, you could start getting that down a lot more.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Analog Components, First Person Flying and Idea Ownership

claims.claim_text: Electron-beam wafer patterning is a raster-based scan rather than a vector process, using multiple beams and increasingly exotic resist chemistries applied on top of the wafer.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's actually a raster. It's not a vector thing. It's a raster-based scan.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Ben & Jeri Show

claims.claim_text: Because wafers come in fixed diameters such as 150 mm and 300 mm, only a fixed number of die fit on each one, so daily chip throughput is set by wafer diameter against die size.
claims.quote_verbatim: wafers are a certain size. You know, they might be 150 millimeters, 300 millimeters in diameter. And you can only fit X amount of chips on that one
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cores, Digikey, Electronic Design - The Commercial Competitor Commencement

claims.claim_text: Fab economics depend on running the line at the highest possible utilisation, on the order of 90 to 95 percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's as high utilization as you possibly can. So 90, 95%.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cores, Digikey, Electronic Design - The Commercial Competitor Commencement

claims.claim_text: The number of test vectors needed for a chip scales roughly with the square of its complexity, so test cost rises faster than device size.
claims.quote_verbatim: as complexity goes up, I think it goes up by like the square, the number of test vectors you need
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cores, Digikey, Electronic Design - The Commercial Competitor Commencement

claims.claim_text: A company that owns its own fab is capped by that fab's wafer starts, for example 20,000 wafers a week, and must allocate them among customers; this capacity ceiling produced the classic 40-week lead time and is a principal reason chip companies moved to fabless models using foundries such as TSMC and UMC.
claims.quote_verbatim: If Maxim had their own chip fabs, then you're limited by that. You can start, you know, 20,000 wafers a week.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: BASIC, Chip companies & Robots - Pernicious Projects, Puppies in Peril

claims.claim_text: LED manufacture continued on four-inch (100 mm) wafers long after logic had moved to much larger diameters.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're they're still using four inch with i mean they they call them 100 millimeter but uh four inch wafers right now for leds
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Bob Pease, Jim Williams - Posthumous Pease Porridge

claims.claim_text: Hobby-scale silicon processing can be reduced to a furnace or pottery kiln capable of 1,000 degrees C, replacing the racks of dedicated diffusion equipment used in a production fab.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I've actually reduced it down to just a furnace that can go to a thousand degrees C or a kiln.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: A CPU fan with double-sided tape can serve as a spin coater for small wafer pieces in a home semiconductor process.
claims.quote_verbatim: And a CPU fan for doing all the spin coating with some double stick tape on it so you can stick the wafer pieces down.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Cut vinyl stickers applied directly to the wafer can substitute for photolithographic masking at hobby feature sizes.
claims.quote_verbatim: And I'm using vinyl stickers currently for all my masking steps.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Oxide etching outside a fab can be done with consumer products containing dilute hydrofluoric acid, such as glass etchant or a rust and stain remover containing 2 percent hydrofluoric acid.
claims.quote_verbatim: rust and stain remover, which happens to have 2% hydrofluoric acid in it
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Production fabs choose the strongest practical acid concentration for oxide etch because throughput dominates, whereas a hobbyist can accept a 20-minute etch with a far weaker chemistry.
claims.quote_verbatim: So if you need to etch an oxide off, they're going to use the strongest acid with the strongest concentration possible so they can just run hundreds of thousands of wafers through per hour.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: The thermal steps of silicon processing dominate its energy cost: running a furnace at 1,000 degrees C for six hours to make a small solar cell consumes more energy than the cell will ever return.
claims.quote_verbatim: The amount of energy that this little solar cell is going to produce, you know, will never repay the amount of energy you put in to run this furnace.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Production fabs amortise thermal processing by holding furnaces continuously at temperature and feeding wafers through without cooldown, driving the energy cost per wafer down to fractions of a penny.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you have a factory where you keep the furnaces up to temperature and you're constantly feeding wafers in there, you can get that cost per BTU down to, you know, fractions of pennies.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Distributing plasma or wet chemistry uniformly becomes the limiting difficulty as wafer diameter grows: on a 2-inch or 4-inch wafer the reaction can be concentrated in one region, whereas 18-inch wafers demand uniformity across a far larger area.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you're doing a 2-inch wafer or a 4-inch wafer, you only have to concentrate it. Like, you can have plasma all over the place, but you only have to concentrate it in one spot, really. But when you're doing, you know, 18 inches across
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: The sole motivation for moving to larger wafer diameters is more die per wafer, which lowers the per-device cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only reason to go to a wafer this big is so that you get more chips per wafer, and you lower the cost of your devices
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: A new leading-edge fab costs on the order of five to ten billion dollars, and the first company to reach a node can price its chips at a large premium for the years before competitors can match it.
claims.quote_verbatim: If Intel gets to 10 nanometers first and it takes them $10 billion to build a new fab
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: OSHW, Makerbot & Memristo - Maundering Memristor Mathematicaster

claims.claim_text: Cree performed all of its LED wafer fabrication and epitaxial layer growth at its Durham, North Carolina site.
claims.quote_verbatim: Every wafer is made here. Every epi layer is grown here in Durham.
claims.speaker: John Edmond
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: After wafer fabrication, LED wafers are diced and the individual die are encapsulated or packaged before being assembled into products such as large display boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they take the wafer and they cut it up and they encapsulate it, package it
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: Wafer probe throughput is raised by multi-probe testers that lower multiple sensor heads and drivers at once so several die are measured in parallel.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can have a multi-probe machine that comes down with multiple sensors for each one
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: A six-inch LED wafer carrying about a million die takes a day or two to test, so a fab keeps hundreds of testers running in parallel to avoid stockpiling untested wafers.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you actually manufacture one wafer with a million on there and then it takes a day or two to test it?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: Moving a design to a smaller geometry shrinks the die and therefore increases the number of parts per wafer, which is the underlying cost argument for a process migration.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you go to a smaller geometry, remember you also get, you get smaller dye so you can get more on a wafer
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gouging Green Gardyloo

claims.claim_text: For very large die at the start of a product's life, yield can be so poor that the useful metric inverts from die per wafer to wafers per die.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't talk about die per wafer. You talk about wafers per die.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Wafers progressively contaminate dry etch chambers, so the quartz kits inside must be periodically swapped out; the chamber then has to be pumped down, tested and verified before it returns to service.
claims.quote_verbatim: eventually, wafers dirty up the chambers, right? And eventually, you have to switch out these quartz kits that are inside of them. This is for, you know, dry etch.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Prototyping, Machining & Accelerators- Mugwumps Mulling Milling

claims.claim_text: Because a fab line is designed for 100 percent utilisation, a single tool going down costs both lost capacity and a growing queue of work-in-progress wafers behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Not only do you have the lack of capacity, but you have this big pile building up behind it, because it's designed for 100% utilization
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Prototyping, Machining & Accelerators- Mugwumps Mulling Milling

claims.claim_text: The minimum practical production run for an analog part is about twelve wafers, which on modern 8-inch foundry wafers already yields a very large number of parts relative to initial demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: So about the minimum run that you can do is 12 wafers
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Holding a die bank of already-fabricated, untested die lets a supplier build finished parts in four to six weeks instead of waiting for a full wafer start.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then you make use, in today's world, liberally of dye bank. So from dye bank, you can build out in 4 to 5 or 6 weeks
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: The cost balance of an analog part has shifted so that packaging now generally exceeds die cost, reversing the older situation of four-inch wafers and five-micron geometries where the die dominated.
claims.quote_verbatim: So in general terms, the definite cost is more in the packaging than it is the dye today.
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Etch equipment moved from effectively open-air chambers to high-vacuum systems because fine geometries cannot be produced without high vacuum.
claims.quote_verbatim: these days, they're like vacuum chambers, and, you know, you have to have, like, really high vacuum to get all these good geometries and everything. We didn't have to previously. They used to be open air, effectively.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Intel, EPA & Brown Field - Google's Ground Gurgitation

claims.claim_text: Die area drives yield, so the larger the die the greater the risk that yield is too low for the part to be commercially viable; this is why very large devices such as FPGAs are rolled out cautiously.
claims.quote_verbatim: The larger the die, the more risk you take that your yield's going to be low.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hardware, Surveys and Giveaways - Radular Rental Ranting

claims.claim_text: Wafer fabrication and packaging are commonly performed on different continents, with probe-tested wafers packed into boxes and shipped overseas for assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they just pack the wafers in cardboard boxes and off they go, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: In plasma etching the wafer is placed in a reactor, pumped down to near vacuum, and exposed to reactive gases that an RF field dissociates so the fragments chemically attack the target film.
claims.quote_verbatim: you put your wafer in the reactor, you pump it down to near a vacuum, and you inject reacting gases, and you bombard them with an RF field so that the molecules fall apart and they react with whatever you want to eat
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Wet etching persisted alongside plasma etching during the transition period, but most process steps had switched to plasma by the time open etch chambers disappeared.
claims.quote_verbatim: We still had wet etching at the time, but most of the stuff had switched over to plasma etching.
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Direct-write patterning that rasters a beam back and forth must be performed wafer by wafer, which is why it has never displaced projection photolithography for volume production.
claims.quote_verbatim: because doing that rastering back and forth, you would have to do that on a wafer basis
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: Early-1980s wafers were only around three and a half inches across and process quality was poor enough that a run might produce only a couple of good die.
claims.quote_verbatim: Here's your two good die off the wafer.
claims.speaker: Bil Herd
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Bil Herd - Zany Z80 Zygology

claims.claim_text: Volume wafer diameters reached 11 to 12 inches, with an industry push toward 18-inch, 450 mm wafers.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're moving to 18, actually. The 450 millimeter.
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Bil Herd - Zany Z80 Zygology

claims.claim_text: An existing part can be shrunk onto a newer process so that more die fit per wafer, a cost-reduction step distinct from designing a new device at a finer node.
claims.quote_verbatim: They'll switch it to a new process and they'll make it smaller so they can fit more of them on a wafer.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: There is no low-commitment, self-service equivalent of cloud computing for silicon: a foundry engagement starts in the region of $300,000 for a lot of wafers, which excludes small startups.
claims.quote_verbatim: our starter tier is $300,000 for a lot of wafers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: Only a very shallow layer at the top of a wafer contains the processed devices; the remaining thickness is undoped bulk silicon, which is why backside access reaches essentially pure silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's very, very small amount of depth from the top of the wafer to the bottom of the processed area. And then the rest is just silicon below it.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: A memory fab in Austin sourced its bare wafers from Japan and its equipment and process chemicals from Japan, Germany and the United States, then shipped finished tested wafers to Korea and on to the Philippines or China for dicing, packaging and final test.
claims.quote_verbatim: We would source all of our wafers from Japan.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: World Trade Futurity (WTF)

claims.claim_text: Analog processes on four-inch wafers historically produced a couple of hundred die per wafer; process and efficiency improvements later raised that to thousands and up to 50,000 die on the same diameter.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd have maybe a couple hundred dye on a four-inch wafer in the old analog days or analog processes, and now you get thousands to 50,000 dye
claims.speaker: Art Kay
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Art Kay

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor lead times, historically quoted at 40 weeks and more recently at 14, represent the whole flow starting from bare wafers rather than a shipping delay.
claims.quote_verbatim: that lead time represents, it's, they're starting with bare wafers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Not Reely An Issue

claims.claim_text: Vendors that hold no finished stock quote lead times reflecting wafer starts, so a customer must plan orders months ahead of running out.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's doing wafer starts, right? You're, you're starting from sand and you're basically getting all the chips you need
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Debugger vs Printeffer

claims.claim_text: New 50 mm (two-inch) wafers can be bought in low quantity from suppliers such as University Wafer for about ten dollars each, giving known specifications, whereas surplus wafers bought secondhand often come with no reliable information about what they are.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a company called University Wafer. And I use two inch wafers, 50 millimeter wafers for most of my stuff. I think in low quantity, they're about 10 bucks each
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: The dopant type of an unlabelled wafer can be determined after purchase by measuring parameters such as resistivity.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a couple easy ways to test what dopant type it is once you've gotten it. You can check parameters like the resistivity
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Ion implantation ionises a dopant gas in a plasma, focuses it into a beam and accelerates it to around 100 kilovolts or more so the phosphorus or boron atoms embed themselves in the silicon at precisely controlled positions.
claims.quote_verbatim: you start with that gas, you ionize it in a plasma, just like the sputtering before you focus into a beam and you accelerate it to a really high potential and normally a hundred kilovolts to even higher
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: The dopant gases used in ion implantation are lethal at concentrations around 50 parts per million and can be absorbed through the skin, which puts them out of reach of amateur processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's, it's something like 50 part per million, um, can be absorbed through your skin and you, and you would die
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: A wafer has no intrinsic origin coordinate, so layer-to-layer alignment during photolithography is the critical constraint on a multi-mask process.
claims.quote_verbatim: You don't really have a zero, zero on a wafer.
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: With positive photoresist the areas blacked out on the mask block UV and their resist is washed away in the developer, while with negative resist the exposed areas remain, so mask polarity must match the resist chemistry.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're using positive photo resist, um, every area that's black on the mask will prevent the UV light from going through in that area and the resist will not be exposed
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Foundries offer hot lots and expedited wafer starts that jump the queue, but when demand surges and every order is marked urgent the mechanism loses its meaning.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can try and get a hot lot or you can try and get expedited, jump the line
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Lowest Common Denominator Design

claims.claim_text: During the 2020-2021 shortage, semiconductor suppliers quoted normal product lead times of 16 to 20 weeks and asked customers for at least 12 weeks of backlog visibility because they could not expedite every order.
claims.quote_verbatim: our normal product lead time is 16 to 20 weeks. And they're saying, can you please at least give us 12 weeks of backlog visibility?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Lowest Common Denominator Design

claims.claim_text: Wafer-in to wafer-out processing alone took about 30 days in one fab, before probe test, overseas packaging, further testing and distribution are added, which is why chip lead times cannot be compressed the way a PCB order can be turned around in 24 hours.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was like a 30 day start to finish, you know, wafer in, wafer out kind of thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Lowest Common Denominator Design

claims.claim_text: A typical fab process flow exposes the wafer in photolithography, rinses it, then passes it to dry ash, so a single broken tool stalls every lot behind that step.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got a photolithography process where they're, you know, basically they're exposing a wafer and then they rinse it and then it's supposed to go to dry ash
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Lowest Common Denominator Design

claims.claim_text: Modern fabs move wafers between process tools with overhead robotic transport systems that can span a dozen separate buildings.
claims.quote_verbatim: this overhead robot system, which basically just transports wafers like through like 12 different buildings
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Lowest Common Denominator Design

claims.claim_text: A plasma etch chamber works by loading a wafer, admitting process gases and striking a plasma with RF generators; the resulting reactive cloud consumes silicon, polysilicon or resist and is drawn away by a turbo pump beneath the wafer.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's like you put a wafer in and then you pump in a bunch of gas and then you turn on the RF generators and then that strikes a plasma.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: A power failure in an etch bay drops the suspended reactive cloud straight onto the wafers below, and at fine geometries anything in process that cannot be cleaned immediately becomes scrap.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've, you've pretty much anything that's in process, unless you can like possibly clean it off immediately, it's scrap
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: An etch tool holds wafers in FOUP pods of about 25 wafers each, with several pods and several process chambers loaded at once, so hundreds of wafers are at risk in a single machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: like had like three chambers of, so like three pods or foops that were like 25 wafers each
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: Obsolete-part suppliers such as Rochester Electronics obtain wafers under agreement from the original vendor and then package and test them themselves to supply finished chips for parts designed in the 1980s.
claims.quote_verbatim: they actually take this, the wafers that they've got and they actually package them up. They will actually package them and test them and, you know, sell you a finished chip for this obscure chip from the 1980s.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: New fab construction in the United States has targeted leading-edge nodes, while the capacity that shortages actually exposed was in legacy lines running 100 mm wafers and older geometries that had been moved offshore because they no longer made financial sense domestically.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want some of the Silicon Valley plants that are doing like 300 nanometer or sorry, a hundred millimeter wafers and stuff like that
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: A die of two square millimetres gives roughly 21,000 dice per 300 mm wafer, an example of how small die area translates into efficient use of scarce wafer supply.
claims.quote_verbatim: Each die occupates just two square millimeters. Very interesting. And each 300 millimeter wafer yields roughly 21,000 dice.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bubblegum Tap Shoes

claims.claim_text: Analog Devices sited a fab in Ireland partly because wafers can be flown in and finished chips flown out cheaply, and the resulting cluster attracted further semiconductor investment and graduates.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's easy to fly in wafers and easy to fly out chips.
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Low seismic activity is a fab siting requirement because ground movement disrupts lithography alignment; porous limestone bedrock that absorbs vibration is an advantage.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're trying to build a fab and you have, you have these little shakes and you're trying to align your lithography machinery, it's not, not going to go so well.
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Buying a dedicated mask set for a whole wafer at 65 nm costs a couple of hundred thousand pounds, which puts a private tape-out beyond a university research group.
claims.quote_verbatim: were to buy a whole mask set for an ADC, uh, for, for, for, you know, for a whole wafer, you know, it would cost at 65 nanometer, a couple of hundred grand
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Multi-project wafer services let several research groups commit a few times a year to a fixed area of silicon each, sharing one mask set and the resulting wafers; Europractice provides this in Europe and MOSIS in the United States, farming the combined design out to foundries such as TSMC.
claims.quote_verbatim: So this company in Europe is called Europractice. I think there's a similar thing in the U S called Moses.
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: The standard multi-project wafer slot is 4 mm by 4 mm, and services occasionally subdivide it further to offer a single square millimetre for about three and a half thousand pounds, which returns around a hundred packaged chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the standard NPW is four millimeters by four millimeters.
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Wafers are shipped between countries between process steps, with different sites performing wafer growth, lithography, packaging and test, because each region specialises in a different part of the flow.
claims.quote_verbatim: Wafers are shipped all around the world to different sites who do different processes on the wafers.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Same Wavelength

claims.claim_text: Silicon ingots, from which bare wafers are sliced, came predominantly from Japan and the supplier base for them is very small.
claims.quote_verbatim: The ingots came from Japan.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Same Wavelength

claims.claim_text: Fabs negotiate power service contracts with liability clauses because a supply interruption destroys every wafer in process, and their large continuous load gives them bargaining leverage.
claims.quote_verbatim: because if the power goes out, all those wafers get destroyed. And I think the power company had some liability in there
claims.episode_title: The Smart Grid with Paul Zawada

claims.claim_text: Mask cost dominates a small silicon run: even a roughly 20-year-old process such as Sky 130 carries a mask cost of about $200,000, after which per-wafer and per-die costs are comparatively low.
claims.quote_verbatim: even an old process like Sky 130, which is about 20 years old, the mask cost is about $200,000
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: A shuttle run places all participants' designs on a single mask so the mask cost is shared, for example $200,000 across 40 participants; every wafer receives a shot of that same combined mask, stepped repeatedly, and the die are sorted at dicing so each participant receives only their own.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you split that 200 grand across 40 people.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: Tiny Tapeout subdivides a single multi-project wafer slot into 250 further slots, pushing the cost of an individual silicon design down another order of magnitude.
claims.quote_verbatim: So in our one slot on an MPW, we have 250 slots.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: Large chip customers hold negotiated wafer allocations that foundries trim under shortage, whereas a small customer can absorb odd spare wafers a foundry offers, which insulated a low-volume part during the 2021-2022 shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have like a wafer allocation and that just got trimmed
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Pre-buying wafers ahead of demand protected stock of the RP2040, where one wafer carries about 20,000 chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's 20,000 chips of wafer
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Extreme ultraviolet lithography is the patterning method needed for the smallest feature sizes on a wafer, but the industry first extended older wavelengths through double, triple and quadruple patterning where that was the more economical high-volume route.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's the methodology for doing patterning on a wafer, right? And so, that was the only way you're going to get down to, like, the smallest sizes you need. But then they went to double patterning in lithography and then triple and quadruple and whatever.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Good Energy Citizen

claims.claim_text: Devices placed close together on one die match each other well, but their absolute values move from wafer to wafer by as much as 10 percent because process variation such as a few microns of extra film thickness alters device performance.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can be very well matched, but they won't match on the next wafer that is produced. They might be like 10% off in value.
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Analog integrated circuits are therefore designed around ratios between components rather than absolute component values, so that a resistive divider still produces the intended output when every resistor shifts together on the next wafer.
claims.quote_verbatim: No, you do it by designing with ratios. So like you do the ratios between components, not precise values of components.
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: A fab is financed by a multi-billion-dollar loan against the building and equipment and then repays it by selling wafers, so prices on a process tend to fall as it becomes trailing edge and the machinery is paid off.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get your massive loan for billions of dollars and then you build your fab and buy all your machinery. And then you're basically selling wafers until you've paid off all the machines.
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: In volume production every chip is tested individually after the wafer is sawn and the die packaged, and the resulting tester data is monitored continuously as a process health signal.
claims.quote_verbatim: every time you saw your wafer up, you put it in, uh, in its package, uh, and then you, then you put it in a tester and it does a ton of tests on each chip
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Package qualification is repeated periodically during mass production to confirm that package materials and quality are not introducing new failures.
claims.quote_verbatim: what we call package qualification, uh, fairly regularly just to check that the, the kind of quality of the package, the materials aren't causing any issues
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A silicon run on the Sky 130 process costs roughly $200,000 to $300,000, which shared among about 40 eFabless participants gives a slot price near $10,000.
claims.quote_verbatim: doing an actual run to make silicon wafers costs, you know, 200 to 300k, at least with the Sky 130 process.
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Subdividing an eFabless slot further brings the price of a custom silicon design to about $200, at which point the participant receives a PCB with their packaged chip mounted and ready to use.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get back a PCB board with your chip mounted on it and ready to go
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: No existing facility performs the whole flow in one place: a fab produces the silicon wafer and then exports it, typically to Malaysia for packaging and elsewhere for die bonding, so a single-campus soup-to-nuts plant would be a departure from current practice.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fab does the silicon wafer and then they export them to Malaysia to get them packaged
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hyper Growth and OpenClaw Interns

claims.claim_text: Custom process development is slow because many lots must be processed wafer by wafer and the resulting defects are distributed, making it hard to separate a design error from a tool error; a company that does not own its fab is also dependent on the foundry scheduling it in.
claims.quote_verbatim: you process them wafer by wafer and the mistakes are, are distributed
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: The Terahertz Frontier with Greg Charvat of Teradar

claims.claim_text: After building several sensor-on-chip companies, the recommended approach is to minimise reliance on custom process steps and leverage standard high-volume processes, locating the competitive advantage in design, applications and test rather than in the process itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think the way to go is you want to use stuff, leverage things that other people are using as much as possible.
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: The Terahertz Frontier with Greg Charvat of Teradar
